items.q: What are the 4 Cs of food hygiene?
items.correct: Cleaning, Cooking, Chilling, and avoiding Cross-contamination.
items.why: Students guess at the Cs. They specifically address the four food-safety risks: dirty surfaces, undercooked food, warm storage, and pathogens transferring between foods (raw to ready-to-eat).

items.q: Which method of heat transfer cooks food in a microwave?
items.correct: Radiation — microwaves are electromagnetic radiation that makes polar water molecules vibrate, generating heat.
items.misconception: Microwaves cook food from the inside out.
items.why: Microwaves penetrate ~1–2 cm into food and excite water molecules — they cook outer regions first, conducting heat inward. The 'inside out' myth comes from feeling cool outer surfaces after microwaving (because steam carries heat out).

items.q: On a traffic-light label, what does a red light indicate?
items.correct: High amounts of that nutrient per 100g - eat less often.
items.misconception: The food is dangerous and should never be eaten.
items.why: Students treat red as 'forbidden'. Traffic lights are a guidance system - red = high, eat less often or in small portions. Many foods (cheese, olive oil) are red on certain nutrients but fine in moderation.

items.q: Does searing meat at the start of cooking lock the juices inside?
items.correct: No - searing creates flavour and colour through the Maillard reaction; it does not stop moisture loss.
items.misconception: Yes - the browned crust acts as a seal that keeps all the juices in.
items.random_wrong: Searing replaces the juices with oil.
items.why: This myth dates back over a century and has been disproved by weighing meat before and after cooking - seared meat loses just as much moisture. Sear for the delicious browned-crust flavour, and rest meat after cooking so juices redistribute.

items.q: Does microwaving vegetables destroy more nutrients than boiling them?
items.correct: No - quick microwaving with little water typically retains MORE vitamin C than boiling, where vitamins leach into the water.
items.misconception: Yes - microwaves 'zap' all the vitamins out of food.
items.why: Students distrust microwaves. Nutrient loss depends on time, temperature and water used - microwaving is fast and nearly waterless, so water-soluble vitamins survive better than in a long boil. Microwaves heat food; they do not make it radioactive.

items.q: How many portions of fruit and veg a day are recommended?
items.why: The answer examiners want is: 5. “10” is the distractor this question was built around — if it tempted you, that's the exact gap to close.

items.q: Eatwell Guide is from which country?
items.why: Correct answer: UK. “USA” sounds right because it borrows the language of the topic — but it fails this question. Re-read the notes on why.

items.q: Recommended portions of oily fish per week?
items.why: Exact answer: 1 portion. Estimation gets you near it; only the anchored number survives the exam hall.
